content: Cystic fibrosis is a genetic condition characterized by the production of abnormal mucus in the lungs, which predisposes individuals to persistent infections. Pulmonary exacerbations occur when infection-related symptoms worsen significantly. Antibiotics are a cornerstone of treatment for these exacerbations. Inhaled antibiotics can be used alone for milder cases or in combination with oral or intravenous antibiotics for more severe infections. Unlike intravenous antibiotics, inhaled antibiotics do not cause systemic side effects and may be a viable option for individuals with limited venous access. This review updates a previously published analysis. The objective of this review was to evaluate whether inhaled antibiotics improve quality of life, reduce time away from work or school, and enhance long-term lung function in individuals with cystic fibrosis experiencing pulmonary exacerbations. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis Group's Trials Register, ClinicalTrials.gov, the Australia and New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform. The last searches were conducted on March 7, 2022, and May 3, 2022, respectively. The review included randomized controlled trials involving individuals with cystic fibrosis and pulmonary exacerbations. These trials compared inhaled antibiotics to placebo, standard treatment, or other inhaled antibiotics over a treatment period of one to four weeks. Two independent reviewers assessed trial eligibility, evaluated the risk of bias, and extracted data. The certainty of the evidence was graded using the GRADE criteria. Authors of the included trials were contacted for additional information. Five trials involving 183 participants were included in the review. Two trials (77 participants) compared inhaled antibiotics alone to intravenous antibiotics alone, while three trials (106 participants) compared a combination of inhaled and intravenous antibiotics to intravenous antibiotics alone. The trials varied in design, and two were only available as abstracts. Assessing the risk of bias was challenging, but four out of five trials were judged to have a high risk of bias due to lack of blinding, and randomization methods were unclear. Reporting of results was incomplete, and limited data were available for analysis. One trial used a cross-over design, and only data from the first intervention arm were included. Inhaled antibiotics alone versus intravenous antibiotics alone: One trial (18 participants) reported a perceived improvement in quality of life in both groups, but the evidence was of very low certainty. Neither trial reported data on time off work or school. Both trials measured lung function, but no differences were observed between the treatment groups (very low-certainty evidence). Regarding secondary outcomes, one trial (18 participants) found no difference in the need for additional antibiotics, while another trial (59 participants) reported no difference in the time to the next exacerbation (both very low-certainty evidence). One trial (18 participants) assessed adverse events and sputum microbiology but found no differences between the treatment groups for either outcome (very low-certainty evidence). Inhaled antibiotics plus intravenous antibiotics versus intravenous antibiotics alone: The combination of inhaled and intravenous antibiotics may have little or no impact on quality of life compared to intravenous antibiotics alone. None of the trials reported data on time off work or school. All three trials measured lung function, but no differences were observed between groups in forced expiratory volume in one second (two trials; 44 participants; very low-certainty evidence) or vital capacity (one trial; 62 participants). None of the trials reported on the need for additional antibiotics. The combination of inhaled and intravenous antibiotics may have little or no effect on the time to the next exacerbation. One trial (28 participants) reported no differences in hospital admissions between groups. There was likely no difference in adverse events between groups (very low-certainty evidence). One trial (62 participants) found no difference in the emergence of antibiotic-resistant organisms (very low-certainty evidence). Authors' conclusions: The evidence available to evaluate the effectiveness of inhaled antibiotics for treating pulmonary exacerbations in individuals with cystic fibrosis is of low or very low certainty. The included trials were underpowered to achieve their objectives, making it impossible to determine whether one treatment is superior to another. Further research is necessary to establish whether inhaled tobramycin could serve as an alternative to intravenous tobramycin for certain pulmonary exacerbations.
